title: The Quantum Hamming Bound in Arbitrary Local Dimension
abstract: The quantum Hamming bound is the finite-length sphere-packing count for exact quantum error correction: the code dimension times the number of correctable local error patterns must fit inside the ambient Hilbert space. For nondegenerate codes this follows from disjoint error spheres. Degeneracy is the only obstruction, because distinct physical errors can coincide on the code subspace and turn sphere packing into an overcount. The central finite-length question has been whether this overcount can ever invalidate the Hamming inequality. Earlier linear-programming, asymptotic, and structural results left a pointwise finite-length problem for arbitrary exact subspace codes. Writing $Q=q^2$ for the Hamming-scheme alphabet, the nonbinary range begins at $Q=9$; here we prove the bound for every $q\ge3$, while the binary endpoint is governed by a distinct $Q=4$ charging geometry. For every nontrivial exact subspace code in this range, any possible violation reduces to a two-center Hamming-ball intersection inequality normalized by the Lloyd response. For $q\ge4$, the Lloyd-square linear program has a uniform half-gap after reduction to alphabet $Q\ge16$ and critical length $n=4t+1$. Qutrits form the boundary: the half-gap disappears, but the bridge is handled by a quadratic-filtered Lloyd square, an exact coefficient-certificate reduction, and a Stein-tangent positivity argument. Thus degeneracy may merge error sectors, but not enough to beat the Hamming count. This proves the nonbinary part of the finite-length quantum Hamming bound; together with the independent binary endpoint theorem, it gives the result in arbitrary local dimension.
summary: This theoretical paper rigorously proves the finite-length quantum Hamming bound for error-correcting codes in arbitrary local dimensions. It achieves this by overcoming the complication of code degeneracy using sophisticated mathematical tools, including linear programming and advanced polynomial analysis. The result establishes a fundamental limit on how many distinct errors can be corrected within a given Hilbert space dimension.
main_problem: The paper aims to prove the finite-length quantum Hamming bound for exact subspace codes in arbitrary local dimension ($q \ge 3$).
main_result: It proves that degeneracy, while potentially merging error sectors, is insufficient to violate the established quantum Hamming count, thereby establishing the nonbinary part of the finite-length quantum Hamming bound.
method: The proof employs advanced techniques including linear programming (LP) bounds, analyzing two-center Hamming-ball intersection inequalities normalized by the Lloyd response, and utilizing specialized algebraic tools like quadratic filtering and Stein's method for specific regimes.
model_or_system: The model is quantum error correction applied to exact subspace codes defined over an alphabet of size $Q=q^2$. The problem is framed as a sphere-packing count within the ambient Hilbert space.
key_observables: Quantum Hamming Bound inequality, $	ext{V}_t^{(Q)}(n)$, two-center intersection ratio $	ext{R}_{Q;n,t}(s)$, and various polynomial signs ($	ext{PII} \ge 0$).
important_parameters: Local dimension $q$ (specifically $q \ge 3$), error weight limit $t$, code length $n$, and the overlap parameter $s$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on reducing the problem to explicit Hamming-scheme inequalities, treating the $q=3$ case separately due to loss of margin, and assuming the validity of complex algebraic positivity checks.
figures_summary: Not specified; the notes refer extensively to equations (e.g., Eq. 1, Eq. 4) and sections detailing algebraic data tables for coefficient verification.
paper_structure: The paper systematically tackles the bound by first establishing general LP reductions, then proving the nonbinary case ($q \ge 3$) via analysis of high-alphabet regimes and a specialized 'bridge window' for qutrits, culminating in the full result by combining with independent binary results.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical machinery developed—combining algebraic geometry (Sturm sequences), spectral theory (Jacobi matrices), and coding bounds—provides deep insights into the fundamental limits of quantum information processing.
